source: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the AI Act) as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (the Digital Omnibus on AI, in force 27 July 2026). Simplified and illustrative, not legal advice.

dateLabels.prohibitionsNew: New bans on intimate-image and child abuse generators
dateLabels.gpaiLegacy: General-purpose AI models already on the market
dateLabels.transparencyLegacy: Marking content from generators already on the market

prohibitions.label: Subliminal, manipulative or deceptive techniques that materially distort behaviour and cause significant harm
Exploiting vulnerabilities due to age, disability or social or economic situation, causing significant harm
Creating or manipulating intimate images of identifiable people without their consent
Social scoring that leads to unjustified or unrelated detrimental treatment
Predicting that a person will commit a crime based solely on profiling or personality traits
Building facial recognition databases by untargeted scraping of images from the internet or CCTV
Emotion recognition in a workplace or educational institution, other than for medical or safety reasons
Biometric categorisation to infer race, political opinions, trade union membership, beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation
Real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces for law enforcement, outside the narrow exceptions

annex3.label: Biometrics: remote identification, categorisation or emotion recognition (where not banned)
Safety component in critical infrastructure: digital infrastructure, road traffic, water, gas, heating or electricity
uk: the sector regulator, for example Ofgem or Ofwat

annex3.label: Education: admissions, grading, assessing the right level of education, or monitoring tests
Employment: recruitment, filtering applications, promotion, termination, task allocation or performance monitoring
Public authorities deciding eligibility for public assistance benefits and services
Creditworthiness or credit scoring of individuals (not fraud detection)
Risk assessment and pricing for life or health insurance
Evaluating emergency calls, dispatching emergency services or triaging patients
uk: the relevant health or emergency service regulator

annex3.label: Law enforcement uses, such as assessing risk of becoming a victim or the reliability of evidence
Administration of justice, or influencing elections and voting behaviour

derogations.label: It performs a narrow procedural task
It improves the result of a human activity already completed
It detects decision patterns or deviations, without replacing or influencing a completed human assessment without proper human review
It performs a preparatory task for an assessment in an Annex III use

obligations.text: Take measures to support the AI literacy of staff and others who operate or use the system for you
Run a risk management system across the whole life cycle
Govern training, validation and testing data, including checks for bias
Draw up technical documentation (a simplified form is allowed for SMEs and small mid-caps)
Build in automatic logging of events
Give deployers clear instructions for use
Design the system so people can oversee it effectively
Achieve appropriate accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
Operate a quality management system (proportionate for SMEs and small mid-caps)
Keep documentation for 10 years and keep the logs under your control
Complete the conformity assessment, sign the EU declaration of conformity and affix the CE marking
Register the system in the EU database before placing it on the market
Take corrective action, and inform others, if the system stops conforming
Monitor the system after it is placed on the market
Report serious incidents to the market surveillance authority
Use the system in line with the provider's instructions
Give human oversight to people with the competence, training and authority to do it
Make sure input data you control is relevant and sufficiently representative
Monitor how it operates, and tell the provider and authorities about risks and serious incidents
Keep the automatically generated logs for at least six months
Inform workers' representatives and affected workers before using it at work
Tell people when they are subject to decisions the system makes or helps to make
Be ready to explain the system's role in a decision to an affected person who asks
Register your use of the system in the EU database
Carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use
Document why the system is not high-risk before placing it on the market, and give the assessment to authorities on request
Register the system in the EU database (simplified content)
Make sure people are told they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious
Mark generated audio, images, video and text in a machine-readable way so they can be detected as AI-generated
Tell people exposed to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation
Disclose deepfakes, and AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest unless it has human editorial control
Keep technical documentation for the AI Office and give information to providers who build on the model
Put in place a policy to comply with EU copyright law
Publish a sufficiently detailed summary of the content used for training
Notify the Commission that the model meets the systemic-risk threshold
Evaluate and test the model, assess and mitigate systemic risks, report serious incidents and protect cybersecurity

ukBaseline: The UK has no cross-sector AI statute in force. The government's approach asks existing regulators to apply five principles within their remits: safety, security and robustness; appropriate transparency and explainability; fairness; accountability and governance; and contestability and redress.

Existing law still applies: data protection (UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, overseen by the ICO, including the rules on solely automated decisions as amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025), equality law (Equality Act 2010) and consumer protection law.
ukTransparency: Chatbots and generated content: consumer protection law (the CMA) and, for online services, the Online Safety Act 2023 (Ofcom) may be relevant.
ukAnnex1: Products: the relevant UK product safety regime and regulator, for example the MHRA for medical devices.
